ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The original data collection, ethical approval, and participant recruitment procedures are described in Kosch et al. (2022) and are not reproduced here.
(2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzle task under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AI assistance).
In their Experiment 2, one hundred participants completed a word puzzle (anagram) task under two counterbalanced within-subjects conditions.
table.header: 2.2 Expectancy Effects and the AI Placebo in HCI

table.text: In the Control condition, participants were explicitly told they would receive no AI assistance and that puzzle difficulty was random.
table.header: 2.2 Expectancy Effects and the AI Placebo in HCI

table.text: In the AI Placebo condition, participants were led to believe that a sophisticated AI was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals such as heart rate and facial expressions, to adapt puzzle difficulty in real time and optimise their performance.
table.header: 2.2 Expectancy Effects and the AI Placebo in HCI

table.text: In the Control condition, participants were explicitly informed that no AI assistance would be provided and that puzzle difficulty was randomly assigned.

In the AI Placebo condition, participants were told that an AI system was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals (heart rate, facial expressions) in real time to adapt puzzle difficulty and optimise their performance.
This model tests the hypothesis that the placebo effect operates purely by changing how certain participants are about their performance expectations.
The experiment employed a within-subjects design with N = 100 participants recruited, of whom N = 75 were retained after preprocessing (see Section 5.2).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> (2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzle task under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AI assistance).

> In their Experiment 2, one hundred participants completed a word puzzle (anagram) task under two counterbalanced within-subjects conditions.

> In the Control condition, participants were explicitly told they would receive no AI assistance and that puzzle difficulty was random.

> In the AI Placebo condition, participants were led to believe that a sophisticated AI was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals such as heart rate and facial expressions, to adapt puzzle difficulty in real time and optimise their performance.

> In the Control condition, participants were explicitly informed that no AI assistance would be provided and that puzzle difficulty was randomly assigned.

> In the AI Placebo condition, participants were told that an AI system was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals (heart rate, facial expressions) in real time to adapt puzzle difficulty and optimise their performance.

> This model tests the hypothesis that the placebo effect operates purely by changing how certain participants are about their performance expectations.

> The experiment employed a within-subjects design with N = 100 participants recruited, of whom N = 75 were retained after preprocessing (see Section 5.2).

Ethics approval statement:

> The original data collection, ethical approval, and participant recruitment procedures are described in Kosch et al. (2022) and are not reproduced here.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository's files are grouped: the repository separates out a study (ex1) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.
#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 53 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (53). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Careless Responding

4 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.


**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: (2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzle task under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AI assistance).
In their Experiment 2, one hundred participants completed a word puzzle (anagram) task under two counterbalanced within-subjects conditions.
In the Control condition, participants were explicitly told they would receive no AI assistance and that puzzle difficulty was random.

In the AI Placebo condition, participants were led to believe that a sophisticated AI was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals such as heart rate and facial expressions, to adapt puzzle difficulty in real time and optimise their performance.
In the Control condition, participants were explicitly informed that no AI assistance would be provided and that puzzle difficulty was randomly assigned.

In the AI Placebo condition, participants were told that an AI system was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals (heart rate, facial expressions) in real time to adapt puzzle difficulty and optimise their performance.
This model tests the hypothesis that the placebo effect operates purely by changing how certain participants are about their performance expectations.
The experiment employed a within-subjects design with N = 100 participants recruited, of whom N = 75 were retained after preprocessing (see Section 5.2).

Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.** - Analsysis_PCO_PUB_FINAL.R reads /usr/local/lib/R/site-library/extrafontdb/metrics/DejaVuMathTeXGyre.afm.gz. No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit. 1. Add the file to the deposit. 2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here("data", "survey.csv") does this for you. 3. Remove any setwd() lines. **Your code was written for older versions of its packages.** - Analysis_code.ipynb: "AttributeError: module 'matplotlib.style' has no attribute 'core'" A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today's version of the package. 1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file. 2. State your version of R or Python in the README. 3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions. ### Other problems in the files - Analsysis_PCO_PUB_FINAL.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.

info.title: Computational Mechanisms of the AI Placebo Effect: A Bayesian Re-Analysis of Expectation-Driven Performance in Human-Computer Interaction

text.text: The AI placebo effect, whereby the mere belief in artificial intelligence assistance alters user expectations and task performance, is an established phenomenon in human-computer interaction (HCI).
Yet the cognitive mechanisms linking placebo beliefs to objective behavioural outcomes remain poorly understood.
This study applies a hierarchical Bayesian computational framework to re-analyse data from Kosch et al.
(2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzle task under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AI assistance).

We compared three models in which the AI placebo manipulation altered either (a) the mean of a prior performance expectation distribution (Shift model), (b) the precision (inverse variance) of that distribution (Precision model), or (c) both simultaneously (Combined model).
Bayesian model comparison via Leave-One-Out cross-validation strongly favoured the Combined model (elpd_diff = 7.11 over the next-best model).

Despite the winning model, group-level analyses revealed no statistically reliable average shift in either prior mean or precision due to the placebo manipulation (95% HDIs broadly overlapping zero), mirroring the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al.

Crucially, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean shift was strongly and positively correlated with observed performance improvement (r = 0.973, p < .0001), explaining the individual-level expectancy-performance relationship originally observed.
text.formatted: Crucially, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean shift was strongly and positively correlated with observed performance improvement (r = 0.973, p < .0001), explaining the individual-level expectancy-performance relationship originally observed.

text.text: Unexpectedly, reduced prior precision (not increased precision) was associated with greater performance gains under the placebo (r = 0.595, p < .0001).
text.formatted: Unexpectedly, reduced prior precision (not increased precision) was associated with greater performance gains under the placebo (r = 0.595, p < .0001).

text.text: These findings provide the first demonstration that hierarchical Bayesian models originally developed to explain placebo analgesia can successfully account for individual differences in the AI placebo effect on objective task performance.
The results indicate that the cognitive mechanism involves simultaneous modulation of both expectation level and expectation certainty, yet manifests highly heterogeneously across participants.
We discuss implications for theories of expectancy-driven performance and for HCI evaluation methodology.

Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly embedded in everyday human-computer interaction (HCI), from productivity tools and recommendation engines to healthcare decision support and adaptive interfaces.
Evaluating whether such systems genuinely improve user performance requires rigorous experimental methodology.
A critical, and often overlooked, confound in this evaluation is the possibility that observed performance benefits arise not from the system itself, but from users' beliefs about what it can do.

This phenomenon, the AI placebo effect, mirrors the well-documented medical placebo effect: just as inert treatments can produce real physiological and psychological benefits when patients believe in their efficacy, the mere belief that an AI is providing support can elevate user expectations and alter task outcomes. Kosch et al. (2022) provided the foundational empirical demonstration of this effect in HCI, showing that participants told a sham AI was adapting puzzle difficulty to their physiological signals performed descriptively better and held significantly higher performance expectations than those in a control condition, despite no actual AI assistance being provided.
text.formatted: This phenomenon, the AI placebo effect, mirrors the well-documented medical placebo effect: just as inert treatments can produce real physiological and psychological benefits when patients believe in their efficacy, the mere belief that an AI is providing support can elevate user expectations and alter task outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref> provided the foundational empirical demonstration of this effect in HCI, showing that participants told a sham AI was adapting puzzle difficulty to their physiological signals performed descriptively better and held significantly higher performance expectations than those in a control condition, despite no actual AI assistance being provided.

text.text: While Kosch et al. (2022) established that the AI placebo effect exists and influences subjective expectations, the cognitive architecture linking belief to objective performance remains unspecified.
text.formatted: While <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref> established that the AI placebo effect exists and influences subjective expectations, the cognitive architecture linking belief to objective performance remains unspecified.

text.text: In particular, it is unclear whether the placebo primarily shifts the mean of users' performance expectations, alters the precision (certainty) of those expectations, or involves both processes.

Moreover, the marked discrepancy between a null group-level performance effect and significant individual-level expectancy-performance correlations suggests substantial heterogeneity that group-mean analyses cannot capture.
Second, the cognitive mechanism linking belief to performance was not modelled: it remains unclear how this so called placebo effect manifests itself.

A productive route to addressing these questions lies in the Bayesian computational frameworks developed in the pain placebo literature. Anchisi and Zanon (2015), building on predictivecoding accounts of placebo analgesia (Büchel et al., 2014), formalised the idea that perceived or observed outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory (or performance) evidence.
text.formatted: A productive route to addressing these questions lies in the Bayesian computational frameworks developed in the pain placebo literature. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anchisi and Zanon (2015)</ref>, building on predictivecoding accounts of placebo analgesia <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Büchel et al., 2014)</ref>, formalised the idea that perceived or observed outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory (or performance) evidence.

text.text: Under this account, a placebo can alter the posterior estimate of outcome either by shifting the mean of the prior distribution, by changing its precision, or by doing both.

These models have successfully accounted for individual differences in placebo magnitude in clinical and experimental pain settings, precisely because they treat expectation level and expectation certainty as separable, quantifiable parameters.

The present study therefore constitutes a direct test of whether the same computational architecture that accounts for expectancy-driven changes in pain perception can also explain expectancy-driven changes in task performance within an HCI context.
The present study applies this modelling approach to the AI placebo effect in HCI.
We re-analyse the Kosch et al.

(2022, Experiment 2) dataset within a hierarchical Bayesian framework in which objective task performance is formalised as the product of Bayesian inference: a prior expectation distribution is combined with a likelihood representing baseline ability.

Under this formalisation, the AI placebo manipulation can affect performance by shifting the mean of the prior (raising the expected performance level), by altering its precision (changing the certainty of expectations), or through a combination of both.

We compare three competing model specifications-Shift-only, Precision-only, and Combined-using Bayesian model selection, and then examine whether the winning model's latent parameters correlate with individual differences in observed performance change.
By importing and adapting computational models originally developed to explain placebo analgesia, this study moves beyond merely demonstrating that the AI placebo effect exists.

It tests whether the same cognitive architecture that accounts for expectancy-driven changes in pain perception can meaningfully explain and quantitatively characterise expectancy-driven changes in task performance within an HCI setting.

The findings have implications both for theories of expectancy-driven performance and for the design of HCI evaluation studies, where uncontrolled expectancy effects may systematically distort conclusions about a technology's true utility.
2 Background and Related Work

The placebo effect refers to real, measurable changes in health, perception, or behaviour that arise from a patient's belief in an inert treatment rather than any pharmacologically active substance (Büchel et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The placebo effect refers to real, measurable changes in health, perception, or behaviour that arise from a patient's belief in an inert treatment rather than any pharmacologically active substance <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Büchel et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Mechanistically, placebo responses involve expectancy-driven modulation of neurobiological systems: positive expectations can activate endogenous opioid pathways, reduce pain-related neural activation, and improve outcomes across a wide range of conditions.

Critically, the magnitude of the placebo response is shaped both by the strength of the prior expectation and by how certain the individual is about the expected outcome, a distinction that maps directly onto the Bayesian framework employed in the present study. Anchisi and Zanon (2015) formalised this within a Bayesian framework, proposing that perceived outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory evidence.
text.formatted: Critically, the magnitude of the placebo response is shaped both by the strength of the prior expectation and by how certain the individual is about the expected outcome, a distinction that maps directly onto the Bayesian framework employed in the present study. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anchisi and Zanon (2015)</ref> formalised this within a Bayesian framework, proposing that perceived outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory evidence.

text.text: Under this account, a strong, high-certainty prior expectation of improvement, the kind induced by a convincing placebo, shifts the posterior estimate of outcome in the direction of the prior, yielding real changes in subjectively and objectively measured performance.
This Bayesian framing provides a principled theoretical basis for applying a similar model to AI-mediated HCI contexts.
User expectations are central to established technology acceptance frameworks.

The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; Davis, 1989) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT; Venkatesh et al., 2003) both identify perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) as primary drivers of technology adoption and satisfaction.
text.formatted: The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Davis, 1989)</ref> and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Venkatesh et al., 2003)</ref> both identify perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) as primary drivers of technology adoption and satisfaction.

text.text: If AI placebo effects artificially inflate these perceptions by making a system seem more capable than it is, evaluations grounded in these frameworks will yield misleading conclusions about a technology's genuine utility.
The susceptibility of technology users to expectancy effects has been demonstrated across multiple paradigms.

How an AI is described, whether as helpful, neutral, or even as a threat, substantially alters users' trust, perceived effectiveness, and subjective satisfaction, even when the underlying system behaviour is held constant.

Users often develop strong mental models of AI capabilities that are shaped more by framing and prior beliefs than by actual system performance. Kosch et al. (2022) provided the most direct and rigorous demonstration of an AI placebo effect in HCI.
text.formatted: Users often develop strong mental models of AI capabilities that are shaped more by framing and prior beliefs than by actual system performance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref> provided the most direct and rigorous demonstration of an AI placebo effect in HCI.

text.text: In their Experiment 2, one hundred participants completed a word puzzle (anagram) task under two counterbalanced within-subjects conditions.
In the Control condition, participants were explicitly told they would receive no AI assistance and that puzzle difficulty was random.

In the AI Placebo condition, participants were led to believe that a sophisticated AI was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals such as heart rate and facial expressions, to adapt puzzle difficulty in real time and optimise their performance.
Critically, no such AI analysis or adaptation occurred; the system behaved identically in both conditions.
Before each block, participants stated their numeric performance expectancy (the number of puzzles they expected to solve out of 40).
Objective performance was recorded as the number of correctly solved anagrams.
The key findings of Kosch et al.
(2022, Experiment 2) were threefold.
First, the AI placebo manipulation significantly elevated participants' pre-interaction performance expectancy ratings relative to the control condition (H1 supported).

Second, despite this clear increase in subjective expectations, there was no statistically significant difference in the average number of correctly solved anagrams between conditions at the group level (H2 not supported).

Third, a significant positive correlation emerged between individual participants' pre-interaction expectancy ratings and their subsequent objective performance, a correlation that was notably stronger in the AI Placebo condition than in the Control condition.

This pattern, a clear subjective effect without a reliable group-level objective effect, yet a meaningful individual-level relationship between expectancy and performance, suggests that the AI placebo operates heterogeneously across individuals.

Understanding why some people's beliefs translate into performance gains while others' do not requires a model of the cognitive process linking expectation to performance, rather than a test of mean differences between groups.
Bayesian frameworks have been applied productively in cognitive science to model how prior beliefs combine with incoming evidence to produce perception, decision-making, and action.

In the context of performance and pain, Anchisi and Zanon (2015) demonstrated that a Bayesian integration model, in which prior expectations combine with a performance likelihood in a precision-weighted fashion, could account for the relationship between expectancy and observed outcomes in placebo-controlled studies.
text.formatted: In the context of performance and pain, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anchisi and Zanon (2015)</ref> demonstrated that a Bayesian integration model, in which prior expectations combine with a performance likelihood in a precision-weighted fashion, could account for the relationship between expectancy and observed outcomes in placebo-controlled studies.

text.text: Applied to HCI performance, this framework formalises the intuition that a participant's final performance on a task reflects not just their underlying ability (captured by the likelihood), but also the influence of their expectations (the prior).

The strength of this prior's influence depends on its precision: a high-certainty expectation (narrow prior distribution) will pull the posterior strongly toward the expected value, while a low-certainty expectation (wide prior) will allow the likelihood to dominate.

This distinction between mean-level effects (where the prior is centred) and precision-level effects (how tightly the prior constrains the posterior) is the central theoretical question of the present study.

The Combined model, which allows the placebo manipulation to affect both the mean and the precision of the prior expectation distribution, will provide a superior account of the objective performance data relative to models that allow only a mean shift or only a precision change.
Support for this hypothesis would indicate that the dual-parameter architecture developed for placebo analgesia transfers successfully to the AI placebo effect in HCI.

The estimated prior mean shift parameter (p shift ) will be significantly greater (more positive) in the Placebo condition compared to the Control condition, reflecting inflated performance expectations induced by the belief in AI assistance.
The individual difference in the estimated p shift parameter (Placebo -Control) will be positively correlated with the individual difference in objective task performance (Placebo -Control).
Participants whose effective prior mean is shifted more positively by the placebo are expected to show greater performance gains relative to their control performance.
In the Control condition, participants were explicitly informed that no AI assistance would be provided and that puzzle difficulty was randomly assigned.

In the AI Placebo condition, participants were told that an AI system was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals (heart rate, facial expressions) in real time to adapt puzzle difficulty and optimise their performance.
In reality, no such analysis or adaptation occurred; the system behaved identically to the Control condition.
Three variables were extracted from the dataset for the present analysis.
The participant identifier (id) distinguished individual participants.
The expectancy variable captured the participant's numeric self-report of expected correct answers (ranging from 0 to 40), recorded immediately before each task block.
The outcome variable (numcorrectanswers) was the objective count of correctly solved anagrams in each block (also ranging from 0 to 40).
The dataset was restricted to observations from the Control ('nothing') and AI Placebo ('camera') conditions.

Data were restructured from long to wide format so that each participant contributed a single row containing their expectancy and performance scores for both conditions (yielding columns expect_Control, expect_Placebo, perf_Control, and perf_Placebo).
Participants with missing values on any of these four variables were excluded listwise.
This yielded a final analytic sample of N = 75 participants.

Two derived variables were then computed: a performance difference score (perf_diff = perf_Placebo -perf_Control) reflecting each participant's placebo-related performance change, and a baseline performance estimate (baseline_perf_data) computed as the mean of perf_Control and perf_Placebo across conditions.
We adopt a Bayesian modelling approach in which objective task performance is treated as the product of Bayesian inference.

Specifically, a participant's observed performance is conceptualised as a posterior distribution arising from the precision-weighted combination of a prior expectation distribution and a likelihood representing baseline task ability.
This formalises the intuition that performance on any given trial is influenced both by what the participant expects (the prior) and by their underlying competence (the likelihood):
Both the prior and the likelihood are modelled as Gaussian distributions.
The prior expectation distribution has mean µ prior and variance σ 2  prior , informed by the participant's stated expectancy rating.
The likelihood has mean µ likelihood (set to the participant's average performance across both conditions) and a fixed variance σ 2 likelihood (set to the observed overall data variance).
The posterior distribution over performance is then derived analytically from the combination of these two Gaussians, and observed performance is modelled as drawn from this posterior.
Three hierarchical Bayesian models were specified, differing in which aspects of the prior expectation distribution were allowed to vary between the Control and Placebo conditions.

In all models, observed performance was treated as a draw from a Gaussian posterior formed by the precision-weighted combination of a prior expectation distribution and a fixed likelihood (baseline ability).
The models differed solely in how the prior was parameterised across conditions: • Shift model.
Only the mean of the prior (µ prior ) was allowed to differ between the Control and Placebo conditions via a participant-level shift parameter p shift .
Prior variance (σ 2  prior ) was held constant across conditions.
This model tests the hypothesis that the AI placebo effect operates purely by raising (or lowering) the expected performance level.
• Precision model.
Only the precision (inverse variance) of the prior was allowed to differ between conditions, implemented via a participant-level log-variance scale parameter log _var_scale.
The prior mean was held constant across conditions.
This model tests the hypothesis that the placebo effect operates purely by changing how certain participants are about their performance expectations.
• Combined model.
Both the prior mean (via p shift ) and the prior precision (via log _var_scale) were allowed to vary freely between the Control and Placebo conditions at the participant level.
This model tests the hypothesis that the AI placebo effect involves simultaneous modulation of both expectation level and expectation certainty.
All three models were implemented in PyMC using non-centred parameterisation to improve sampling efficiency.
Group-level hyperpriors were weakly informative Normal distributions for means and HalfNormal distributions for standard deviations.
The analysis code is available at https://osf.io/54ut2/overview.
text.formatted: The analysis code is available at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/54ut2/overview">https://osf.io/54ut2/overview</ref>.

text.text: All three models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling implemented via PyMC's No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS).
For each model, four independent chains were run with 2,500 posterior samples each, following 2,500 tuning (warm-up) steps.
The tar-get_accept parameter was set to 0.98 to encourage careful exploration of the posterior.
A fixed random seed was used for reproducibility.
Log-likelihood values for the observed performance variables were computed and stored for model comparison.
To address RQ1 and test H1, the three models were compared using Leave-One-Out crossvalidation (LOO), calculated via ArviZ's az.compare function.
LOO estimates the expected log-predictive density (elpd_loo), which quantifies out-of-sample predictive accuracy while penalising model complexity.
Pointwise log-likelihood values across both observed performance variables (perf_ctrl_obs and perf_plac_obs) were summed per participant and passed to the comparison function.
Models were ranked by elpd_loo; the model with the highest (least negative) value was identified as the best-fitting model.
Model weights were also examined.
All subsequent hypothesis testing was conducted using posterior samples from the best-fitting model identified through model comparison.

For H2, group-level posterior distributions of the condition difference parameters (∆_group_mu_p_shift and ∆_group_mu_log_var_scale) were examined using posterior means, 95% Highest Density Intervals (HDIs), and the posterior probability that the difference exceeded zero.
For H3, participant-level posterior means of the condition difference parameters were extracted and correlated with the observed perf_diff score using Pearson's r.
All three models converged satisfactorily.
The Shift model showed no divergent transitions, a maximum R of 1.000, and minimum ESS values of 6,685 (bulk) and 5,593 (tail).
The Precision model also showed no divergences, a maximum R of 1.000, and minimum ESS values of 3,848 (bulk) and 1,903 (tail).
The Combined model produced one divergence across all chains and draws, a negligible number, with a maximum R of 1.000 and minimum ESS values of 3,189 (bulk) and 5,228 (tail).
All models were therefore considered to have achieved reliable posterior estimates suitable for interpretation and comparison.
Table 1 presents the LOO model comparison results.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> presents the LOO model comparison results.

text.text: The Combined model, which allows both the prior mean and prior variance to vary between conditions, achieved the highest elpd_loo score (-473.03) and captured essentially all available model weight (≈ 1.0).
The difference in elpd_loo between the Combined and the next-best model (Precision only) was 7.11 standard error units (SE_diff = 1.41), constituting strong evidence in favour of the Combined model.
The Shift-only model performed considerably worse than both alternatives.
Table 2 presents the posterior distributions of the group-level mean differences between the Placebo and Control conditions for both parameters of the Combined model.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> presents the posterior distributions of the group-level mean differences between the Placebo and Control conditions for both parameters of the Combined model.

text.text: These null group-level findings parallel the null effect on average objective performance  reported by Kosch et al. (2022), and are consistent with the interpretation that the AI placebo effect does not operate uniformly across individuals.
Despite the null group-level results, strong individual-level relationships emerged between estimated parameter changes and observed performance changes.
Table 3 summarises these results.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> summarises these results.

text.text: Taken together, the results indicate that (a) the Combined Bayesian model best characterises the performance data; (b) at the group level, the placebo manipulation does not produce reliable average shifts in either prior mean or precision; but (c) at the individual level, the degree to which each participant's prior mean shifts positively is a powerful predictor of performance gain, and, unexpectedly, the degree to which prior precision decreases is also positively associated with performance improvement.

This study provides the first formal test of whether hierarchical Bayesian models of expectancy originally developed in the pain placebo literature can account for the AI placebo effect on objective task performance.

The results support a dual-mechanism account: the best-fitting model is one in which the placebo belief simultaneously modulates both the mean and the precision of participants' prior performance expectations.
At the same time, these latent parameter changes show no reliable average shift at the group level, thereby explaining the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al. (2022).
text.formatted: At the same time, these latent parameter changes show no reliable average shift at the group level, thereby explaining the null group-level performance effect reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean is an exceptionally strong predictor of performance improvement (r = 0.973), while an unexpected reduction in prior precision is also positively associated with performance gains.
Together, these findings demonstrate both the transferability of the Bayesian modelling framework across domains and the highly individual-specific nature of the AI placebo effect.
The strong preference for the Combined model over both single-mechanism alternatives indicates that neither mean shifting nor precision change alone is sufficient to account for the data.
This result has an important theoretical implication: the AI placebo effect in HCI cannot be reduced to a simple "raising of the bar" whereby users expect more and thus achieve more.
Instead, the effect simultaneously alters how high the expectation is set and how certain users are about that expectation.

This dual-mechanism picture is consistent with the broader Bayesian theory of placebo effects proposed by Anchisi and Zanon (2015), who emphasised that both the location and the precision of prior beliefs modulate the integration of expectation with incoming performance evidence.
text.formatted: This dual-mechanism picture is consistent with the broader Bayesian theory of placebo effects proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Anchisi and Zanon (2015)</ref>, who emphasised that both the location and the precision of prior beliefs modulate the integration of expectation with incoming performance evidence.

text.text: From a TAM and UTAUT perspective, this finding suggests that AI placebo effects do not simply inflate perceived usefulness (which would correspond to a mean shift in expectation) but may also alter the confidence with which users hold their usefulness beliefs.

If precision changes are not accounted for in standard usability evaluations, the pattern of results, including both inflated satisfaction scores and unexpected individual differences in response to the AI framing, will remain poorly explained.

The successful transfer of this dual-parameter architecture from pain perception to HCI task performance suggests that precision-weighted integration of expectations may be a domain-general mechanism of expectancy-driven behavioural change.

The absence of statistically reliable group-level differences in either p shift or log_var_scale echoes the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al. (2022) and provides a cognitivelevel account of why that null effect arises.
text.formatted: The absence of statistically reliable group-level differences in either p shift or log_var_scale echoes the null group-level performance effect reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref> and provides a cognitivelevel account of why that null effect arises.

text.text: The AI placebo belief does not uniformly recalibrate users' prior expectations upward; instead, some individuals show large positive shifts in their effective prior mean, others show small shifts, and still others may show negative shifts.
When these heterogeneous individual responses are aggregated, they cancel out at the group level.
This has direct practical implications for HCI evaluation methodology.
Standard betweengroup or within-group mean comparisons are inadequate tools for detecting placebo effects that are highly individual-specific.

Researchers evaluating AI systems should supplement meandifference analyses with individual difference approaches, including regression models predicting performance from expectancy, or computational models of the kind demonstrated here, to detect and characterise the full scope of expectancy-driven effects.

The individual-level correlation between prior mean shift and performance change (r = 0.973) is remarkably strong and provides a computationally grounded explanation for the expectancyperformance correlation originally observed by Kosch et al. (2022).
text.formatted: The individual-level correlation between prior mean shift and performance change (r = 0.973) is remarkably strong and provides a computationally grounded explanation for the expectancyperformance correlation originally observed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kosch et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: The Bayesian model attributes this correlation to the mechanism of Bayesian integration: participants who hold a higher-certainty, upward-shifted prior expectation will have their posterior performance estimate pulled more strongly in that direction, yielding better outcomes.

In other words, the extent to which a person genuinely internalises the belief that the AI is helping them, captured here by the estimated shift in their effective prior mean, is the primary determinant of whether the placebo belief translates into performance.
This has implications for understanding individual differences in placebo susceptibility more broadly.

Factors such as dispositional trust in technology, prior experience with AI, suggestibility, and general optimism may all modulate the degree to which the AI placebo framing shifts individuals' prior beliefs.

Future work incorporating these individual difference variables as predictors of the estimated p shift parameter would provide a richer picture of who benefits from, and who is unaffected by, AI placebo effects.
The most theoretically generative finding concerns the direction of the precision-performance relationship.
Contrary to the prediction derived from standard Bayesian placebo models, reduced prior precision (i.e., greater uncertainty) under the AI placebo was associated with larger performance improvements.
This is the opposite of what a standard Bayesian account would predict, in which tighter, higher-precision priors exert stronger influence on the posterior and hence on performance.
Several interpretations of this counterintuitive finding deserve consideration.

One possibility is that, in the context of an anagram task where performance is highly variable and strategydependent, a looser, less certainty-bound expectation facilitates a more exploratory and flexible approach to problem solving.

Rather than locking onto a particular expected outcome and pursuing it rigidly, participants with wider prior distributions may engage more openly with each puzzle, trying alternative strategies when initial approaches fail.
This is consistent with research showing that reduced performance anxiety, itself often associated with lower expectation certainty, can improve performance on cognitively demanding tasks.
A second interpretation is methodological.

The estimated log_var_scale parameters are latent variables inferred from behavioural data, and in a model that simultaneously estimates both mean shift and precision change, there may be identifiability pressures that couple the two parameters in ways that produce artefactual correlations.
The positive association between reduced precision and performance improvement could partly reflect parameter trade-offs rather than a genuine psychological mechanism.

This possibility underscores the importance of replicating the precision finding with direct measures of expectation certainty, for example, by asking participants to provide confidence intervals around their expectancy estimates rather than single-point values.

A third possibility is that the AI placebo manipulation, by framing the task as one in which performance is dynamically adapted to the participant's state, introduces genuine uncertainty about what performance level is appropriate, thereby widening the prior distribution.

Participants who are most responsive to this uncertainty induction, whose prior width expands most, may also be those who engage most actively with the task, leading to better outcomes through increased effort rather than through the precision mechanism per se.

Distinguishing among these interpretations requires future experiments with direct measures of both expectation level and expectation certainty, ideally administered at multiple time points within the task.

The current finding is nevertheless important in flagging that the relationship between expectation precision and performance under AI placebo conditions is non-trivial and not straightforwardly explained by existing theory.

Regardless of which interpretation ultimately proves correct, the result indicates that the relationship between expectation certainty and performance under AI placebo conditions cannot be assumed to mirror the relationship observed in placebo analgesia.
This divergence itself constitutes a theoretically informative boundary condition for Bayesian models of expectancy.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.

First, the study is a re-analysis of existing data and therefore inherits the design constraints of the original experiment, including the specific task (anagram solving), sample characteristics, and experimental procedure.
Generalisability to other task types, populations, or AI interface modalities cannot be assumed without further replication.
Second, the Bayesian model rests on specific structural assumptions, including Gaussian distributions for both the prior and the likelihood, and fixed values for BASE_VAR_PRIOR and VAR_LIKELIHOOD.
Results are contingent on these assumptions, and sensitivity analyses with alternative parameterisations would strengthen confidence in the conclusions.
Third, although convergence diagnostics were satisfactory, LOO warnings about elevated Pareto k values for some observations indicate sensitivity to influential data points.
The conclusions should be interpreted with appropriate caution pending replication.

Fourth, and perhaps most importantly, the model does not incorporate subjective outcome measures (perceived workload, satisfaction) or individual difference variables (personality traits, AI attitudes, cognitive ability).
The hierarchical structure captures individual differences implicitly but does not explain them.
Including such moderators in future models would considerably enrich the account.
Fifth, the correlational nature of the H3 analyses does not license causal conclusions.

The association between estimated parameter changes and performance changes is consistent with a causal mechanism, but alternative explanations, including unmeasured confounds, cannot be ruled out on the basis of correlational data alone.
This study provides the first formal computational characterisation of the cognitive mechanisms underlying the AI placebo effect on objective task performance.
Applying a hierarchical Bayesian framework to data from Kosch et al.

(2022, Experiment 2), we found that the pattern of individual-level expectancy-performance relationships is best explained by a model in which the placebo manipulation simultaneously affects both the mean and the precision of users' prior performance expectations.

At the group level, the manipulation produced no reliable average shift in either parameter, mirroring the null group-level performance effect, but at the individual level, the extent of each participant's prior mean shift was a remarkably strong predictor of their performance gain.

An unexpected finding regarding precision, in which reduced certainty, not increased certainty, was associated with better performance, challenges simple prior-strengthening accounts of the placebo effect and opens a productive theoretical question for future investigation.
More broadly, the present findings illustrate the value of importing formal computational models from related literatures into HCI.

By adapting Bayesian models of placebo analgesia, we were able both to explain a previously puzzling pattern of results and to generate a new theoretical question about the role of expectation uncertainty in performance contexts.

As AI systems become more pervasive, understanding the psychology of AI-induced expectations-and the cognitive architectures that mediate them-will be essential for ensuring that evaluations of these systems reflect genuine capability rather than the beliefs they happen to inspire.

Kosch et al. (2022) established the existence of the AI placebo effect and identified a key puzzle: despite significant manipulation of subjective expectancy, the group-level effect on objective performance was non-significant, while individual-level expectancy-performance correlations were significant and condition-dependent.
This dissociation points to substantial inter-individual variability in how the placebo belief translates into behaviour.

However, the authors did not model the cognitive mechanism responsible for this individual-level relationship, nor did they investigate whether the placebo affected expectation certainty as well as expectation level.
The present study directly addresses this gap by applying a hierarchical Bayesian computational model to the Kosch et al.
(2022, Experiment 2) dataset.

We ask three specific research questions: RQ1: Can a hierarchical Bayesian model that allows the AI placebo to modulate both the mean and the precision of prior performance expectations (the architecture previously successful in modelling placebo analgesia) outperform simpler single-mechanism alternatives in accounting for objective performance data?
RQ2: Does the AI placebo manipulation produce statistically significant average changes in the latent cognitive parameters (prior mean shift and prior log-variance scale) at the group level?

RQ3: Are individual differences in estimated parameter changes between the Placebo and Control conditions significantly correlated with individual differences in observed performance change, providing behavioural validation of the modelled mechanisms?

All models share the same fixed likelihood (baseline ability).
